chapter.title: Tutorial
chapter.para: This chapter is a hands-on introduction to Scaly. It gets you from an empty file to a running program, then takes you on a quick tour of the language. Later chapters cover everything here in depth; the goal now is to write and run real code as fast as possible.

section.title: Building the Compiler from the Seed
section.para: Scaly is self-hosted: the compiler is written in Scaly and compiles itself. It is distributed as a seed — the compiler emitted as its own LLVM IR, the .ll files committed under seed/. A single seed serves every 64-bit little-endian target — the IR carries no target triple, so the compiler you build from it targets whatever machine it runs on. Turning the seed back into a working scalyc needs only LLVM 18 and a C compiler for the final link; no C++ toolchain is involved.
Install the prerequisites, then run the build script from the repository root:
section.programlisting:
; macOS brew install llvm@18
; Ubuntu 24.04 sudo apt install llvm-18 clang-18
tools/build-from-seed.sh
section.para: This compiles the seed with llc, links it into scalyc/build/scalyc, and builds the small runtime archive the compiler links your programs against. For brevity, the rest of this tutorial assumes the compiler is on your PATH:
section.programlisting: export PATH="$PWD/scalyc/build:$PATH"

note.para: The runtime archive lives at /tmp/libscaly.a. If it gets cleared — for example after a reboot — and the compiler reports it missing, just re-run tools/build-from-seed.sh to rebuild it.

section.para: The C++ bootstrap that originally produced the seed is described in ; you do not need it for everyday use.

section.title: Hello, World!
section.para: A Scaly program is just a file of statements — there is no main function to declare and nothing to import. Put this single line in a file called hello.scaly:
section.programlisting: print("Hello, World!")
section.para: Compile it to an executable with -o, then run the result:
section.programlisting: scalyc -o hello hello.scaly ./hello
section.para: The program prints:
That is the whole edit-compile-run loop. Everything that follows is just more interesting things to put between the braces.

section.title: Using Scaly with VS Code
section.para: You can drive the whole edit-compile-run-debug loop from Visual Studio Code: a build task to compile the file you are editing, a run task to execute it, and a launch configuration that stops at breakpoints and lets you step through your Scaly source. Debugging uses the DWARF information the compiler emits with the -g flag, so breakpoints land on real source lines and scalar local variables show their values.
Open the Scaly repository as your workspace folder and install the CodeLLDB extension (extension id vadimcn.vscode-lldb), which provides the lldb debugger type used below.

note.para: Run the compiler with the repository root as the working directory. The prelude (which defines print and friends) is resolved relative to the current directory, so building from elsewhere fails with function not found: print. The tasks below set cwd to ${workspaceFolder} for exactly this reason.

section.title: Setting a Breakpoint and Stepping
section.para: Put this program in area.scaly at the repository root. It computes a rectangle's area from two mutable bindings — small, but enough to stop and inspect some values:
section.programlisting: var width 8 var height 5 var area width * height if area = 40 print("the area is 40") else print("unexpected area")
section.para: Click in the gutter to the left of the var area width * height line to set a breakpoint (a red dot appears), then press F5. The program builds and runs, and execution stops at that line before it executes — at which point width and height already have values but area does not yet.
With execution paused you can:

listitem.para: Read width and height in the Variables pane, or hover them in the editor to see their values.
Step one line at a time with F10 (Step Over) — after stepping past the breakpoint line, area appears with the value 40. Step into a called function with F11.
Press F5 again to continue to the program's end.

section.para: Breakpoints, stepping, and variable inspection all rely on the -g debug information; without it the program still runs, but the debugger has no source lines to stop on.

section.title: Stepping into Functions and the Call Stack
section.para: Stepping becomes more interesting once a function is involved. F10 (Step Over) runs a call as a single step; F11 (Step Into) descends into the called function so you can watch it run. Put this program in rectangle.scaly at the repository root — it factors the area calculation out into a function:
section.programlisting:
function area(w: int, h: int) returns int { var result w * h result }
var width 8 var height 5 var a area(width, height) if a = 40 print("the area is 40") else print("unexpected area")
section.para: Set a breakpoint on the var a area(width, height) line and press F5. When execution stops there, width and height show in the Variables pane. Now press F11 instead of F10: the editor jumps into the body of area and stops on var result w * h.

The Call Stack pane (bottom-left of the Run and Debug view) now lists two frames — area on top and main below it — showing exactly how you got here. Click a frame to switch the Variables pane and the editor to that frame's context: selecting main shows width and height again, while area shows its own local result (still unassigned at this point, just as area was before its line ran in the previous example).
From inside the function you can keep stepping, press Shift+F11 (Step Out) to return to the caller, or F5 to continue to the end. The function-and-procedure model is covered in and .

section.title: What the Debugger Shows
section.para: Debug support tracks the parts of the language that are most useful to inspect today, and is being widened over time. At present:

listitem.para: Breakpoints land on top-level statements, bindings, and function bodies.
The Variables pane shows scalar var locals — integers and booleans — for whichever stack frame is selected.
Function parameters, let (immutable) bindings, and aggregate values such as structures and strings are not shown yet.
Lines inside loop and conditional bodies currently share the location of the enclosing statement, so breakpoints and stepping are coarser there.
The Watch view and Debug Console evaluate expressions as C/C++ and do not understand Scaly names. To read a value, use the Variables pane or hover over the name in the editor.

section.title: A Tour of Scaly
section.para: This section sweeps quickly across the language using small, complete programs. If something is not fully explained here, do not worry — every feature is covered in detail in the rest of this specification, and each part of the tour points you to the relevant chapter.

section.title: Values and Bindings
section.para: Bind a value to a name with let. There is no equals sign — the name is followed directly by its value. Use var for a binding you intend to change, and set to change it. A semicolon starts a comment.
section.programlisting: let answer 42 ; immutable binding var count 0 ; mutable binding set count: count + 1 ; assignment uses a colon
section.para: The equals sign = is reserved for comparison, so it never gets confused with assignment. See for the full lexical rules.

section.title: Operators and Precedence
section.para: Operators are ordinary identifiers, not keywords baked into the grammar. When they are chained, they combine using standard mathematical precedence — multiplication binds tighter than addition:
section.programlisting: ; 3 + 4 * 5 is 3 + 20, which is 23 — not 35 let result 3 + 4 * 5 if result = 23 print("got 23") else print("unexpected")
section.para: Parentheses group explicitly, and an operator written before its operand acts as a prefix function (-x, ~flag). See for the complete model.

section.title: Control Flow
section.para: if chooses between branches. Single-statement branches need no braces; the condition needs no parentheses:
section.programlisting: let n 7 if n < 0 print("negative") else if n = 0 print("zero") else print("positive")
section.para: while repeats as long as its condition holds. Use braces for a multi-statement body:
section.programlisting: var sum 0 var i 1 while i <= 10 { set sum: sum + i set i: i + 1 } ; sum is now 55
section.para: for iterates. for i in 4 runs i from 0 up to — but not including — 4:
section.programlisting: var total 0 for i in 4 set total: total + i ; total is 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6

section.title: Functions
section.para: A function declares its parameter types and return type. The value of the last expression is returned automatically — no return keyword is needed for the final result. A single-expression body needs no braces:
section.programlisting:
function add(a: int, b: int) returns int a + b
let s add(3, 4) ; s is 7
section.para: Functions can call themselves. Here is the classic factorial:
section.programlisting:
function factorial(n: int) returns int if n <= 1 1 else n * factorial(n - 1)
let f factorial(5) ; f is 120
section.para: Functions are pure: they read their arguments and return a value, with no side effects. To mutate, use a procedure.

section.title: Procedures and Mutation
section.para: A procedure is like a function but may change its inputs and perform side effects. The distinction is visible at every call site, so a reader always knows which calls can mutate state. See for the details.

section.title: Structures and Methods
section.para: Define a structure by listing its fields. A structure with public fields gets a constructor that takes them in order. Methods are functions or procedures whose first parameter is this:
covers constructors, including the page-aware init# form used by types that allocate.

section.title: Unions, Options, and choose
section.para: A union holds one of several variants. Each variant may carry a payload. The most common union is Option, which represents a value that may be absent:
Match on a union with choose. Each when clause names a binding, then the variant, then the result; the binding is bound to the variant's payload. An else clause handles the remaining variants:
section.programlisting:
function or_zero(o: Option) returns int choose o when v: Some v else 0
let a or_zero(Option.Some(7)) ; a is 7 let b or_zero(Option.None) ; b is 0
section.para: See for union layout, the T? shorthand, and pattern matching in full.

section.title: Putting It Together
section.para: Let us combine the pieces into one small, complete program: a safe division that returns an Option instead of crashing on a zero divisor, with the caller deciding what to print.
Start with the function. It returns None when the divisor is zero, and Some with the quotient otherwise:
section.programlisting:
define Option union(Some: int, None)
function safe_divide(a: int, b: int) returns Option if b = 0 Option.None else Option.Some(a / b)
section.para: Now call it and react to the result with choose. The Some arm receives the quotient; the else arm handles division by zero:
section.programlisting: let result safe_divide(20, 4) choose result when q: Some if q = 5 print("20 / 4 = 5") else print("unexpected quotient") else print("cannot divide by zero")
section.para: Put both pieces in divide.scaly, then build and run it:
section.programlisting: scalyc -o divide divide.scaly ./divide
section.para: It prints:
Change the call to safe_divide(7, 0) and the same program prints cannot divide by zero — the union makes the failure a value you must handle, not a crash you can forget.
From here, the rest of this specification fills in the details: the rules, the full model, and the system including generics, lifetimes, and region-based memory management.
